text:
David Vance ran a hand over the yellowed photograph of Elias Thorne, a smile frozen just before the man vanished into the Blackwood Bay fog. The police scanner on his desk, usually a reliable source of late-night small-town banality, suddenly sputtered. It wasn't the usual white noise; fragments of sound, impossibly deep and devoid of human inflection, ripped through the air – not words, exactly, but data corrupted, like a digital scream from somewhere beyond the broadcast band. He leaned in, straining to parse the noise, but it dissolved into a flat, unnerving hum.

Then he felt it. A low, persistent vibration resonated through the floorboards, a frequency just below the threshold of normal background noise. It wasn't strong enough to rattle the lamp, but it hummed in his teeth, an almost imperceptible tremor from the very earth beneath the old building. He glanced around, noticing a fresh hairline crack spiderwebbing from the corner of his office window, tracing a faint, stark line across the plaster where none had been yesterday. It looked too neat, too deliberate, as if etched by something with an unnatural patience.

Blackwood Bay was always whispering, but lately, the whispers felt less like rumors and more like encrypted messages. The air itself felt thin, stretched taut over something vast and unseen, and the integrity of everything—information, ground, sanity—felt like it was subtly, irrevocably unraveling.
